variants.title: Follow the contract chain
variants.context: A production pipeline is a chain of contracts: capture records source identity, validate gates quality before transformation, transform applies deterministic versioned logic, materialize writes and then publishes atomically, and consume binds training or serving to an explicit dataset version.
variants.prompt: An order event travels from a mobile client to a model that scores it. Put the pipeline stages in order.

items.text: Consume the published artifact from training, batch scoring, or online serving by explicit version.
Materialize the partition or feature view into an isolated location and publish it only after validation succeeds.
Capture the record with its source, event time, ingestion time, record key, and immutable raw location.
Transform by normalizing, joining, and aggregating with deterministic code and pinned parameters.
Validate schema, freshness, uniqueness, ranges, and domain invariants before any transformation runs.

variants.hint: Which stage still holds a record the pipeline can replay from?
variants.explanation: Capture, validate, transform, materialize, consume. Validating before transformation stops corrupt input from being baked into derived values.

variants.title: Follow the contract chain
variants.context: A production pipeline is a chain of contracts: capture records source identity, validate gates quality before transformation, transform applies deterministic versioned logic, materialize writes and then publishes atomically, and consume binds training or serving to an explicit dataset version.
variants.prompt: An auditor asks where each piece of a partition's evidence was created. Put the stages in the order that produced them.

items.text: The quality results and quarantine counts for the interval are produced.
The training or serving consumer records which artifact version it read.
The source identity, event time, and raw location are recorded.
The output partition and its manifest publication time are written.
The transformation and configuration versions are attached to the run.

variants.hint: Lineage is assembled stage by stage, not reconstructed afterwards.
variants.explanation: Every stage emits the evidence the next one needs, which is what makes a published artifact explainable later.

variants.title: Follow the contract chain
variants.context: A production pipeline is a chain of contracts: capture records source identity, validate gates quality before transformation, transform applies deterministic versioned logic, materialize writes and then publishes atomically, and consume binds training or serving to an explicit dataset version.
variants.prompt: A producer adds a required currency field that changes how amounts are interpreted. Put the stages in order for the work the change creates.

items.text: Consumers move to the new dataset version and record which version they trained or scored on.
Validation adds the field to the contract and rejects records whose currency cannot be resolved.
The transform normalizes amounts using the field instead of assuming a single currency.
Capture begins storing the field with the bumped schema version on the raw record.
Materialization writes a new candidate partition and publishes it only after the checks pass.

variants.hint: A semantic change to units has to be gated before it reaches a feature value.
variants.explanation: Units are part of the schema contract. Interpreting amounts inside the transform without gating the field would silently change every derived value.

variants.title: Apply the event-time policy
variants.context: Event time is when the action happened; processing time is when a worker observed it. Assign event time from the domain contract, group records into windows, advance a watermark as an estimate of event-time progress, then apply the lateness policy for records that arrive after the allowed boundary.
variants.prompt: A delivery app buffers events on a phone that stays offline for twenty minutes. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Advance the watermark as an estimate of how complete event-time progress is.
Assign event time from the event's domain contract rather than from the worker clock.
Apply the lateness policy to the buffered records that arrive after the allowed boundary.
Group the records into the fixed windows the business question asks about.

variants.hint: The worker clock only says when the record was seen.
variants.explanation: Event time, windows, watermark, lateness policy. A watermark is an operational estimate, not proof that no earlier record can arrive.

variants.title: Apply the event-time policy
variants.context: Event time is when the action happened; processing time is when a worker observed it. Assign event time from the domain contract, group records into windows, advance a watermark as an estimate of event-time progress, then apply the lateness policy for records that arrive after the allowed boundary.
variants.prompt: A live ranking signal aggregates a viewer's clicks into session windows. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Place each click into a session window that closes after the configured gap of inactivity.
Advance the watermark so the session can be considered complete enough to publish.
Take the click timestamp from the client event contract, which carries the moment of the click.
Decide, for a click that lands after the allowed lateness, whether to update, retract, or drop it with a measured reason.

variants.hint: Session boundaries are a windowing decision, not a watermark decision.
variants.explanation: Windows answer the business question, the watermark estimates completeness, and only then does the lateness policy apply.

variants.title: Apply the event-time policy
variants.context: Event time is when the action happened; processing time is when a worker observed it. Assign event time from the domain contract, group records into windows, advance a watermark as an estimate of event-time progress, then apply the lateness policy for records that arrive after the allowed boundary.
variants.prompt: One aggregate is published three times: early, on time, and as a correction. Put the steps in order that produce those publications.

items.text: A record arriving inside the allowed lateness triggers a correction that consumers know replaces the earlier value.
The event time on each arriving record fixes which interval it belongs to.
The watermark passes the window end and the on-time result is published.
An early low-latency result is emitted for the open window.

variants.hint: Consumers must know whether an update replaces, retracts, or appends.
variants.explanation: The same aggregate can have several valid publications. The lateness policy defines which of them consumers should trust.

variants.title: Make a retry harmless
variants.context: Replay equivalence means the same logical interval, transform version, schema, and parameters produce the same committed output. Derive run identity from the data and keep the attempt number separate, write a shadow candidate and swap a manifest atomically, and replace partitions or merge by a stable key instead of appending blindly.
variants.prompt: A daily job's run identity is currently derived from the wall-clock time the scheduler fired. A retry therefore produces a second identity for the same data. What should identity be derived from?
options: The dataset, logical interval, transform version, schema version, and parameters, with the attempt number kept separate.
The wall-clock start time plus the attempt number, so every attempt is uniquely traceable.
The output file checksum, since identical data should produce an identical identity.
optionFeedback: Correct: identity names the logical work, so any attempt at the same work resolves to the same output version.
This makes every attempt a different logical dataset, which is exactly the confusion that duplicates data.
A checksum is computed after the work, so it cannot name the work an orchestrator is about to run or retry.
variants.hint: What must stay the same across two attempts at the same work?
variants.explanation: Run identity comes from the data and the code, not from the clock, so a retry resolves to the same intended output.

variants.title: Make a retry harmless
variants.context: Replay equivalence means the same logical interval, transform version, schema, and parameters produce the same committed output. Derive run identity from the data and keep the attempt number separate, write a shadow candidate and swap a manifest atomically, and replace partitions or merge by a stable key instead of appending blindly.
variants.prompt: A transform appends its output rows to a table. After a worker finished writing and then failed before acknowledging success, the interval now holds every row twice. What change fixes this?
options: Disable retries for this task so the orchestrator never runs it twice.
Replace the whole partition, or merge by a stable record key, instead of appending.
Add a deduplication job that runs nightly over the affected tables.
optionFeedback: Retries are normal and a worker can still fail after writing, so removing them trades duplicates for missing data.
Correct: deterministic replacement makes a second run of the same logical task produce the same committed rows.
A nightly cleanup leaves consumers reading duplicated data in between and does not restore replay equivalence.
variants.hint: Which write semantics make a second run of the same work a no-op?
variants.explanation: Blind append turns an ordinary retry into duplicate data. Partition replacement or key-based merge is what makes replay harmless.

variants.title: Make a retry harmless
variants.context: Replay equivalence means the same logical interval, transform version, schema, and parameters produce the same committed output. Derive run identity from the data and keep the attempt number separate, write a shadow candidate and swap a manifest atomically, and replace partitions or merge by a stable key instead of appending blindly.
variants.prompt: A training job occasionally reads a partition while it is still being written and gets a partial result. Which commit protocol fixes it?
options: Write the partition in ascending key order so partial reads always contain a valid prefix.
Write into a temporary location, validate the complete result, then atomically swap the manifest readers resolve.
Have readers sleep and retry until the row count stops changing between two reads.
optionFeedback: A valid prefix is still an incomplete interval, which is exactly what must not reach a training consumer.
Correct: the reader-visible reference only ever points at a validated, complete candidate.
Polling infers completion from a heuristic and still races with a writer that pauses between batches.
variants.hint: What does a reader actually resolve when it opens the dataset?
variants.explanation: Build an isolated candidate, validate it, then publish one reader-visible reference. Readers never see a half-written result.

variants.title: Choose the gate disposition
variants.context: Validation is only a gate when it changes pipeline behavior. Fail closed when the output would violate a consumer contract, leak labels, corrupt identifiers, or train on an incomplete interval. Quarantine malformed records when the valid majority can publish without bias. Warn and continue only when the deviation is understood, bounded, and attached to the published artifact.
variants.prompt: A daily partition is missing four of its twenty-four hourly source files. The transform would still run and the retraining job is scheduled in an hour. What should the gate do?
options: Fail closed, because training on an incomplete interval violates the consumer contract.
Warn and continue, because twenty of twenty-four hours is most of the data.
Quarantine the missing hours and publish the rest as a complete partition.
optionFeedback: Correct: an incomplete interval published as complete is precisely the case for failing closed.
The deviation is neither bounded nor understood, and the consumer would read the partition as a full day.
Missing hours are not malformed records, so there is nothing to quarantine and the label complete would be false.
variants.hint: Would the consumer be able to tell the interval was short?
variants.explanation: Fail closed when the published artifact would misrepresent completeness, because downstream training cannot detect the gap.

variants.title: Choose the gate disposition
variants.context: Validation is only a gate when it changes pipeline behavior. Fail closed when the output would violate a consumer contract, leak labels, corrupt identifiers, or train on an incomplete interval. Quarantine malformed records when the valid majority can publish without bias. Warn and continue only when the deviation is understood, bounded, and attached to the published artifact.
variants.prompt: Three tenths of a percent of records in an interval have an unparseable postal code. The remaining records are unaffected and referential integrity holds. What should the gate do?
options: Fail closed, because any contract violation means the interval cannot be trusted.
Coerce the unparseable values to an empty string so every record can be published.
Quarantine the malformed records with reason codes and publish the valid majority.
optionFeedback: Failing closed on a bounded, isolatable defect blocks a usable interval and creates unnecessary freshness debt.
Coercion hides the source regression and silently changes the meaning of an empty postal code.
Correct: the valid majority can publish without bias, and the rejected records keep evidence for repair.
variants.hint: Can the valid rows be published without biasing the result?
variants.explanation: Quarantine when the defect is isolatable and the majority stays representative, and keep the reason codes so the source can be fixed.

variants.title: Choose the gate disposition
variants.context: Validation is only a gate when it changes pipeline behavior. Fail closed when the output would violate a consumer contract, leak labels, corrupt identifiers, or train on an incomplete interval. Quarantine malformed records when the valid majority can publish without bias. Warn and continue only when the deviation is understood, bounded, and attached to the published artifact.
variants.prompt: Volume for one interval is 12 percent below the reviewed band. The product owner confirms a promotion ended that day and the drop matches the expected traffic change. What should the gate do?
options: Quarantine the interval until volume returns to the reviewed band.
Warn and continue, attaching the reviewed deviation to the published artifact.
Fail closed, because a distribution check outside its band is a contract violation.
optionFeedback: There are no malformed records here, so quarantine would withhold valid data with no repair path.
Correct: the deviation is understood and bounded, and recording it lets downstream users interpret the artifact.
Blocking a correct interval creates freshness debt for a change that is real product behavior, not corruption.
variants.hint: Is the deviation understood and bounded, or unexplained?
variants.explanation: Warn and continue is only safe when a named owner has explained the deviation and the note travels with the artifact.

variants.title: Route the freshness budget
variants.context: Route the freshness budget by starting from the time the consumer must act, subtracting unavoidable source and processing delay, and spending what remains on the publication interval. The simplest mode that fits the remaining budget wins.
variants.prompt: A ranking feature must be visible to serving within 15 minutes of the event. Source delay takes 2 minutes, the transform 3, quality checks 1, and publication 1. How much of the budget is left for the publication interval?
variants.hint: Subtract the unavoidable work from the deadline before choosing a mode.
variants.explanation: The remaining budget is what the publication interval may spend, and it decides whether micro-batch can meet the objective.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the delay that is consumed rather than the budget that remains.
Added the consumed delay to the deadline instead of subtracting it.

variants.title: Route the freshness budget
variants.context: Route the freshness budget by starting from the time the consumer must act, subtracting unavoidable source and processing delay, and spending what remains on the publication interval. The simplest mode that fits the remaining budget wins.
variants.prompt: A risk score must reach an analyst within 30 minutes. The source lags 6 minutes, the transform takes 9, validation 2, and publication 3. How much of the budget is left for the publication interval?
variants.hint: Every stage between the event and the consumer spends part of the deadline.
variants.explanation: Deadline minus source and processing delay gives the interval budget, and a mode that needs more than that cannot meet the objective.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the total consumed delay instead of the remaining budget.
Subtracted only the source lag and ignored the processing stages.

variants.title: Route the freshness budget
variants.context: Route the freshness budget by starting from the time the consumer must act, subtracting unavoidable source and processing delay, and spending what remains on the publication interval. The simplest mode that fits the remaining budget wins.
variants.prompt: In the same 30-minute pipeline, the team optimizes the transform from 9 minutes down to 4. By how many minutes does the remaining publication budget grow?
variants.hint: The gain is the change in one stage, not that stage's new cost.
variants.explanation: Freshness budget is additive, so shortening one stage returns exactly that many minutes to the publication interval.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the new transform cost rather than the improvement.
Added the old and new transform costs instead of taking the difference.
